utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're to continue your examination-in-chief. The witness has been here four full days, and we should be concluding his examination-in-chief today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where the new cemetery was in relation to the village that the soldiers, according to this note, showed to the crime technicians who went there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That new cemetery, according to the note that we read out, was near to the village, in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that the authorised officials from the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and for us just to be reminded of the document we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what document are we using now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the Official Note from tab 404, which we were quoting from at the end of business last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. There is a translation of this single-page document. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already quoted from the document, so I don't want to waste time there. I'm going to ask the general a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what -- the fact -- or, rather, what the officials found at the end of the village, was it a mass grave or a larger number of individual persons buried?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite obviously it wasn't a mass grave. It was a number of people buried individually in one location, and we can call it or refer to as a new cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the officials of the Secretariat of the Interior think about the age of the cemetery and on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the fresh mounds, the officials concluded that it was a new cemetery, recently dug.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when and where, or rather, when and why did they leave the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left the cemetery in a very short space of time. That is to say they spent very little time there because somewhere nearby, as it says in the note, some shooting could be heard from automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they conclude about the religion of the people buried in that cemetery?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They concluded that the people buried there were Muslim, and they were able to deduce that on the basis of the tombstones and the way in which the bodies were facing, the graves were facing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once that cemetery was discovered in Izbica, who did the police inform about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police informed the district prosecutor in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, General, when one establishes a body, even in wartime, and nobody knows whether the person was killed in combat or in some other way, is a criminal report filed and then criminal proceedings or, rather, an investigation undertaken as a result?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Either a criminal report is filed or the authorised public prosecutor is informed about the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, who does the district prosecutor -- who did the district prosecutor in Kosovska Mitrovica turn to when these -- the cemetery was discovered?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district prosecutor went to see the investigating judge of the District Court in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have here in tab 405 a proposal for an order of exhumation, and it is dated the 31st of May, 1999. The current number is 59/99, and we're dealing with tab 405, the next tab.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a document of the district public prosecutor in Kosovska Mitrovica where they refer to the court and propose exhumation, and an order for exhumation which comes under the competence and the authority of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the process is that the district prosecutor proposes to the investigating judge or, rather, to the court to issue an order of exhumation and that the -- each individual case must be investigated for the cause of death to be established. In addition to that, if it is possible to determine the identity of each individual, take the paraffin glove test, make a note of the clothing worn, and that a complete record should be compiled and sent in, and this document is dated the 31st of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the prosecutor proposes all the steps to be taken that I have just read out. And what was the decision pursuant to this request that the investigating judge in -- of the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica made?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He accepted the proposal by the district public prosecutor and did indeed issue an order for exhumation, which we find in tab 406.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tab 406 is the exhumation order issued by the investigating judge of the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here "Exhumation Order" and are all the points listed that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In points 1 to 10, it states specifically what steps are to be taken pursuant to this exhumation order and the event that took place itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to save time, I'm not going to take these points in detail one by one, the different points in the exhumation order, but since you have them in front of you, as I say I'm not going to take it point by point, but can you tell us whether this order contains quite literally all the necessary steps which are customarily taken and must be taken once an investigation of this kind is unleashed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This order is the kind of order containing all the measures that are generally taken faced with an event of this kind,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in the procedure on the part of the state organs, in this case the police and the court, was anything omitted in the general procedure necessary to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from the next few documents that we can see that due to the circumstances some of the measures that were set out were not sufficiently -- or carried out as exactly as would otherwise have been possible had the circumstances been different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me before we go on, when was the exhumation actually conducted pursuant to the exhumation order?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact day, but it should have been the 2nd of June, if I remember correctly. The exhumation, that is, including all the attending steps as stipulated by the order itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the exhumed bodies transferred to and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were transported to Kosovska Mitrovica, and there was a total of 101 exhumed bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an external investigation conducted first of all?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was a post-mortem carried out?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who carried out the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The experts for autopsy from the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where were the bodies buried, the ones that were found?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies found in Izbica, once the post-mortem had been carried out and all the steps pursuant to the exhumation order, were buried in several cemeteries of the Kosovska Mitrovica and Vucitrn municipalities immediately after the autopsies were carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion was a report compiled of the crime scene investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here in tab 407 do we have a report on the field forensic examination which was compiled on the 2nd of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. Yes, that's the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what in this report on a field forensic examination, to be found in tab 407 as we've just said, what does it say about the conditions under which the exhumation was conducted and the other steps that were taken pursuant to the exhumation order?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report states that the exhumation itself was conducted under very complex conditions with the risk of attack from terrorist groups, in fact. So that when the exhumation took place and the examination took place, there was an attack that was launched and one soldier was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, all the members of the team, were they able to go about their business or did they have to deal with their own safety and security?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. They had to see that they were safe and secure because of the conditions surrounding the exhumation process itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what was omitted? What steps were omitted or only partially implemented in view of the prevailing conditions, that is to say that they were under fire in that particular location?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order, they were supposed to mark the gravesites in the same way, in a uniform way, as well as the bodies and all the other documentation. However, due to the circumstances, this was not done in all cases. That is to say the graves and the bodies were not marked in all cases, but it states quite clearly in the reports which body was found in which grave. Apart from that, through force of circumstance once again, the conditions prevailing, prints of the capillary lines were not taken and the so-called paraffin glove test was not done. Possibly something else was omitted but those are the two points that come to mind now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3 of this report, in the description, and I'm going to skip over the fact that it was pursuant to a written order from the court, it says that: "In the Muslim cemetery, which we can -- the character which may be deduced from the names and surnames inscribed on individual gravesites, as well as the fact that the head is turned southward, toward Mecca, 101 gravesites were counted and marked on the chart. The investigating team was able to read inscriptions with the names and surnames on 45 mounds, or gravesites, of which two gravesites bear merely the following markings: CE and Ljavdim. In relation to the inscription CE, which was also barely legible, no hypotheses can be offered with respect to its origin or meaning. The inscription 'Ljavdim' may be the name of the body buried there and it is in fact a name which occurs frequently among members of the Albanian minority, but it may also mean 'glory to him,' 'glory be.' Also, of the inscriptions that could be read, it was noted that there were five where in addition to the name and surname there was also the inscription of 'UCK' or 'KLA.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Milosevic? Mr. Milosevic, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, with respect to the identification process, was a detailed report compiled or, rather, can we see that in this report? Does tab 407 mirror that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In actual fact, an individual review was carried out and compiled of all the bodies and gravesites, and you can see this on page 2, 3, 4, 5, up to the middle of page 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 1 is there any explanation given as to the circumstances under which this assignment was carried out? And I'd like to draw your attention to the last paragraph in which it states, among other things: "We should like to mention that while carrying out our task we were not able to adhere to the plan of work fully and the order in which the procedure was conducted, so that point 4 of the order was not carried out satisfactorily or fully." So I'm asking you whether an explanation is given for that, because it says here: "... because the Muslim cemetery in the village of Izbica is located in the heart of the territory which until recently was under the control of the terrorist OVK, some elements of which apparently have not yet been neutralised."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This talks about the problems that the team for exhumation encountered on the spot, and this explanation begins on the first page and ends in the first third of the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any characteristic points here from which we can see under which conditions, under what kind of conditions they worked?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first page, under sentence 1 we see: "During the exhumation the security detail of the investigation team came under strong fire from infantry weapons and until the investigation team left the site one soldier was wounded." And of course we see later that it caused certain problems in the exhumation itself. And on page 2, we see a more detailed explanation of what the problems were and on which points the order was not fully executed, accompanied by a reasoned explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we read here, among other things, that the graves were marked and some even had bunches of flowers on them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were inscriptions of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to what issue in the indictment is this evidence related?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is related to para -- to the paragraph which explicitly mentions Izbica. I'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have difficulty following this evidence. What I understand is that police received an information from Internet website, but they were not able to find the mass grave. Instead, this is what they have found. But one time I understand the general referred to tab 17. This mass grave -- this grave is located in Kosovska Mitrovica, and you mentioned a place in Pusto Selo. There I have some confusion. If you clarify that, please, General.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, your microphone has to be activated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. The last day of my testimony I did indeed mention Pusto Selo in order to explain that the aerial photograph of the alleged mass grave refers to that village, and it was almost identical. Since we do not have such a photograph in the tab for Izbica but we have a photograph in the tab dealing with Pusto Selo, I just wanted to show the photograph to see what it looks like because the two are almost identical. Here it is in the tab for Pusto Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 420.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 420. We had a similar aerial photograph for Izbica. We don't have it in our tab here, but I know that there exists one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's still not clear; where is this evidence leading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this paragraph 66(g) is something that serves as a basis for a charge of murder. It says that at least 4.500 villagers from Izbica and the surrounding villages took refuge in a meadow. From what it says here, we see that the men were allegedly separated and then killed. All that the general here is saying, and what we can see from the documents, refutes this claim because the documents speak of the way in which those villagers in fact lost their lives. And we also see that the authorities, the judiciary and the police authorities, also conducted an extensive investigation and established first that it was not a mass grave, second, that those were individual graves, and they started an investigation. So the question arises there is a single thing, a single element --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How do the documents speak of the way in which the villagers in fact lost their lives, as you say? That's not clear to me. Which is the issue here. And that's the issue; how did they lose their lives? The indictment alleges that they lost their lives as a result of action taken by the forces of the FRY and Serbia, but how do these documents indicate otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, I quoted from the first page a moment ago where it says clearly that this locality is in the heart of the territory that was until recently held by the KLA, which had not been neutralised by that time yet, and we know that from the fact that they shot at the investigation team. It is reasonable to assume that members of the KLA buried the people who were killed on their side in fighting with the forces from Serbia. There is not a single element to prove the claim made by Mr. Nice. If there were 4.500 villagers, there couldn't have been only 100 men among them. That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if that's your case, that's your case, but it does require a big leap to get to that conclusion, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in which way one can reach the conclusion stated in 66(g), namely that the people were killed. It says that men were separated from women and the men were killed. If there were 4.500 villagers, there couldn't have been only 100 men. It simply doesn't hold water. And second, we see it was in the heart of the territory controlled by the KLA where fighting was going on. There's no single basis for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I merely wanted to find out what your case was on this issue and you have explained it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One should be also guided by certain conclusions regarding the fact that the police conducted an investigation. Why would the police have to conduct an investigation if it had known how those people had died? Why would they have done that? They wanted to obtain some information of what really happened, and that's why they investigated. First of all, we see from these documents that they searched for seven days to find the village in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, [no interpretation] -- [Interpretation] When this indictment was being written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to proceed with your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did continue with any examination. I will let the general see this, and you can even put it on the overhead projector. Mr. Robinson, in the first indictment, which was written -- you know the dates -- it was sometime in May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed with your questions. You've already given the explanation. I mean, what we make of it is a matter for us. I was merely trying to understand the case you were presenting. Proceed with your questions. We're trying to conclude this witness's examination-in-chief today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning of the second third of second page in this report under 407, it says, speaking of the marks, distinction marks found, it says that at the Muslim cemetery in the village of Izbica, not only people from that area were buried but also from other localities. That runs completely counter to the allegations in the indictment, but it supports the claim that it was people killed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have instructed you to proceed with your question. I have instructed you more than once to proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this list of persons who were identified, does it coincide, if you had occasion to compare the two lists, does it coincide with the list given as a schedule in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have an opportunity to compare the two lists, the schedule from the indictment and the list of people who were assumed to be identified, and I noticed considerable differences. Fifteen to 20 names coincide. In this list, there are other names that are not listed in the schedule, and the schedule, on the other hand, contains some names that are not included in this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This exercise having been done in advance of testimony, I expect that a schedule or similar exists showing the match and the non-match of names. It would be helpful to have that. The Chamber will remember that we had similar problems with Racak. The Prosecution landed up doing the work that should have been done by the accused, and with this number of documents for me to deal with, I really don't have any spare resources to turn to exercises like this. So if the witness or the accused has a schedule to reflect the last answer that was obviously known to be an answer coming, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have any schedule that explains the discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, we believed that it is sufficient to provide this entire record from tab 408, and if you allow me, I will read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So beginning with page 2, starting with body 1 until the end, and that's body 101, you have the list of those identified and not identified. And among the identified in the first third of page 3 you have Racaj Saban Ramadan, coincides with the name in the schedule. Isufi Zenelj coincides, Dibran Hadzi, Hoti Rrustem also coincides, Thaci Dervis --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't follow it this fast, I'm sure the Court can't, and if the accused had the courtesy of looking at the Court, he would see that the Court is still trying to find documents as indeed am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your presentation would have been facilitated if you had prepared a list. If you are going to proceed as you have been doing, you have to proceed more deliberately, more slowly. I'm still trying to find the documents. Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, the accused was reading from the B/C/S version, which is in Cyrillic, and therefore it's probably rather harder for English readers to follow the names in Cyrillic than in the Latin script, and it may assist the Court and it may assist me if the accused would be good enough to work from the English version, there now being a translation, and using page numbers of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the best way to deal with this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, have you been following this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've been trying to, but I think we all need some help as to where we're going to see the issue of the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness. General, if you can indicate some of the discrepancies, and then I'm going to ask -- I'm going to instruct the accused, with the help of Mr. Kay, to prepare a list and present it to the Court. General, can you indicate, looking at Schedule F and the list which is in Exhibit 407, some of the discrepancies in the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honour, I cannot at this moment. I know very well that when I compared the two lists I saw where they overlapped in 15 or so cases. I know that I found names on this list that do not exist in the indictment and the other way around. However, unfortunately, I did not deal with the question systematically. What I'm saying now is quite certain: It can be done, but it requires a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you are not in a position to even name the 15 which overlap? Because that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have them marked, 18 names that overlap. From this document in tab 407, 18 names overlap with the schedule in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us the 18 overlapping names, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. On page 3 of this document, in the beginning of the last third, Racaj Saban Ramadan, then a few lines down, Morina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are looking at the English version. Could you identify the corpse number or the English page number. If you could identify the corpse number, it would be easier for us to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mark the English version, only the one that is in tab 407 in the Serbian language. So unfortunately, I cannot help you with that. Perhaps during the break this can be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the Serb version it would appear that the corpses are also numbered. Can you not relate the name to the number of the corpse? That's good enough for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that the corpses were numbered by hand, so I simply don't know whether it was one of my associates who put these numbers from 1 to 101 or whether that's the version that you received too. It must have been one of my associates who simply dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. The document we have in Serbian has 1 to 101 in typewritten numbers, in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. You're right. You're right. One of my associates simply wrote the numbers on the margin of the text so that it would be easier for me, but I see it now in the text itself. So number 30 in the Serbian version, that is Racaj Saban Ramadan. Then number 35 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 35 in the Serbian version. Then number 36, number 39, number 47, number 49, number 55, number 59, number 60, number 69, number 72, number 74, number 82, number 83, number 84, number 86, number 88, and finally on the last page, 93. Those are the names that overlap with the names in Schedule F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, the last one, Salja Tahir Zumber, where do you find in Schedule F of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Salja Tahir Zumber. Now we're going to look him up. Salja Zumber. On the last page -- on the last page of this list in the indictment, the second one. The second name on the last page. Again, there are no numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is "Zumber" and the indictment says "Zymer."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably a technical discrepancy, a mere typo, but he was found here, according to his identity card and his personal identification number. That is how the names were matched. A total of 18 overlap from tab 407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to point something out to you, Mr. Robinson. When we compare the first indictment to the second indictment, 70 names contained in the first indictment are not contained in the second indictment. I can give you the first one where all the names that do not appear in the second indictment at all are marked in red. Then you can look at the second one where I marked in red - or, rather, Professor Rakic was kind enough to do that - a large number of names that are not contained in the first indictment. Indeed, one wonders how this was established, except from KLA sources. It's only the KLA who could have given this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the second indictment which is the final indictment, so they benefited from their experience. The Prosecution, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, I think on the basis of information received on killed members of the KLA, and it's only the KLA that could have provided these figures to them, no one else. How else can you explain the fact that all the victims are males? This is a cheap, senseless explanation that men with separated from women. That is something inconceivable to anyone in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please tell me, do you have any information about anyone separating men from women and executing them anywhere or at any situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to any kind of execution of civilians or military or whoever?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have information about crimes committed by policemen, soldiers, and civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of the persons for whom you have this information were arrested and handed over to a court of law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suppose I ought to make the point that those last three questions, the first two general in the extreme and effectively tendentious or leading and the last one clearly leading, just don't add at all to the material of value before the Chamber. But if the accused chooses to use his time in that way, I'm not going to stand up and object every time he does it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't know whether it's a leading question when I ask whether all persons for whom it was established that they had committed crimes were handed over to the authorities, to the judicial authorities. I assume that the general can give a qualified answer in terms of yes or no. He could have said that the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't stop you. Just proceed with your questions so that we can conclude this examination. It's far too long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree on that with you. It is very long, but there are very many documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in tab 409 there are some sketches, a sketch of the cemetery, I believe. Yes, yes, at the end of tab 409. And also photographs.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are colour photographs there. We've already had a look at them. Can we place these on the overhead projector. Mr. Bonomy said that there were some numbers on one of these colour photographs, numbers from the on-site investigations. Here on the photographs numbers can also be seen. I can't see where they are now. These are close-ups, the colour photographs. So on the original photographs, did you establish, General, that they all have stamps of the Ministry of the Interior, and XVI - have you checked this? - does that correspond to the SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not check that in the meantime because I was mindful of what I was told, not to communicate with anyone while giving testimony, but if need be, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the colour photographs we can clearly see how the graves were marked. It is much clearer than on the black and white photocopies. If you're interested in seeing them, they can be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we do not wish to have them on the projector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are these the same photographs? Are these similar to the ones in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We don't have colour copies unless there are some coming our way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at least you should point out the correspondence between the photographs you have presented and those in tab 409, which have numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How should I put this? They were taken by the same police unit, that is to say the Secretariat of the Interior of Kosovska Mitrovica. My associates received them from the same source, that is to say the Ministry of the Interior. It can be seen in the photographs that they overlap and how. For example, photograph number 7 is totally identical or almost identical to this colour photograph, if you place it on the overhead projector, because you can see that that is photograph number 8. Photographs number 7 and 8 show the same type of marking, and the same general appearance of the graveyard is there. You can see that they were all buried individually. That can be seen on black and white photographs where every tombstone is marked in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in 66(g) it says -- it says everything that I've already quoted to you, that on the 27th of March, 1999, the forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled the village of Izbica, that at least 4.500 villagers from Izbica and surrounding villages took refuge in a meadow. The men were separated and executed. We saw that it says here that 116 were killed. And then I'm drawing your attention to the rest of the text in subparagraph (g): "Also on 28 March, 1999, the women and children gathered at Izbica were forced to leave the area and walk towards Albania." Now, what is derived from this text is that the men were executed, shot, and that out of a total of 4.500 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question? It's not the time for comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, my question is if the men were executed and the women and children deported and there were a total of 4.500 persons, 100 were men only, allegedly, who buried these people if the rest were deported?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. That's a speech. If you carry on in this way, I'll have to terminate the examination-in-chief. That's not a question. That's a comment you can make in your closing address.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on these identified persons do we find markings from which we can see which place the people buried came from?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some of these the geographic area is noted, which should be the place they had come from. I remember a place called Lejocina [phoen] and some others on the tombstones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So places are written up which are not Izbica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask you any more questions about that particular tab. Now, in tab 410, we have the reports on the individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to 410, the colour photographs clearly being distinct from the black and white ones, for good order, if they're going to be produced in due course, might they simply become part of 409? We're likely to forget it if we don't deal with it now. It seems to me, apart from the one the accused referred to, the others don't match photographs and are additional, therefore. I'm not, by suggesting this, conceding their admission, but I would have thought the better course would be for him to amend his file at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, they can be considered in relation to 409, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say for the record that I'm not claiming that the black and white photographs are copies of these here but that these are additional photographs which have on the back the number of the Ministry of the Interior, and they were all taken in the same location, and you can establish that, that they were all on the same site, or at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. At least one matches, but let's move on. We'll consider their admission in relation to tab 409. Tab 410, is that translated? It's a very long --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, all the individual reports on identified and unidentified persons are here. The translations exist of one identified and one unidentified, because there was no need for all these reports to be translated, so just two for purposes of illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we can see here how the authorities functioned, what their work was. And it would be superfluous to translate all of them. So we have one identified and one identified translated and all of them were either one or the other. So this is a pattern --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- according to which the officials worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Do you want us to look at one, one that has been translated which is illustrative of the others?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the whole point. Each individual case is documented. There's a document for every single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the document say how the person died? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's ask the general what documents are contained and what points are referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this tab we have 101 complete report on the findings of the body. Each report contains two pages. The first page, which is titled Report on the discovery of the body, the date of discovery, the time, the place, et cetera, who the officials were who took part in the exercise, and a brief description of the corpse. And then we are referred to page 2 and the second part of the form which makes up this complete document. And in continuation, the word Identified or Unidentified is underlined, and in principle, when reports of this kind are compiled, we tend to underline unidentified regardless of the fact that there is a name on the document because this implies subsequent investigation to check out the facts found on the grave site or confirming them or refuting them. And then at the end it says where the body was buried. That's page 1. Now, in form 2 on page 2 in the upper right-hand corner, we see the number of body, in keeping with the minutes and records previously, and a personal description of the corpse and what the corpse was wearing. Of course there is -- we do not find a description of the elements that represent part of the autopsy or external examination, which comes under forensics and the forensic experts. That is their job. And as we've said, that was done by the team from the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade. And we don't include those documents here; it is the army that has the forensic reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer to my question is no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would be right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it a component part of this investigation and the steps taken to have a -- and the collection of photographs, the photo documentation, compiled for each individual case to be found in tab 118; is that right? Would that include that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For each individual case, that is to say for each grave, we should have a photograph of the grave site and a photograph of each individual body. But in the report that we looked at at the beginning of today's testimony, quite possibly that work was not completed. But anyway, most of those photographs do exist and are to be found in tab 418, if I understood you correctly, and that is the big binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is supplementary documentation. There's no text. It's just photographs, and that entire binder, tab 418, ranges from 1 to 101. So these are all the photographs.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the photographs, yes. Mostly there are more than one photograph for each casualty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The numbers in the picture, which appear in the picture and upper right corner of this tab 410, does this match with the number in -- with the corpse number which we saw in tab 407?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be logical. I can't confirm that just now, but that would be logical, yes. We can see that the first photographs are marked with number 1 or, rather, the first is number 1 and the last is 101, so I think that I can confirm that that is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in view of this extensive investigation, on-site investigation, the exhaustive descriptions, the proceedings on the part of the prosecutor, the investigating judge, the photo documentation and everything else, all these documents and all these steps taken, can it be linked with any assertions that those persons were executed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. On the basis of all my knowledge, I would say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when all these activities were taking place, was there any knowledge whatsoever that some crime had been perpetrated there? Did anything lead you to suspect that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall police investigation and the forensic investigation was there to establish that, and the procedure is still ongoing, to establish or refute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, under those circumstances, you were in Kosovo for a large portion of the war, did the investigative authorities and police, could they have done anything else, taken any other steps in this case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, they did the maximum that was possible, given the prevailing circumstances, because the essence of this is that this material serves as a basis, and the case is still open. It's not a shut case yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, during the identification process, did they use information from the uniform information system, data system?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that tab 412 shows us that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go on to that. What system is this, General? Could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A uniform information system of the MUP of Serbia is a database about all citizens of the Republic of Serbia, including all personal data about the citizens, including their status, whether they have passports, IDs, driving licenses, et cetera. So in that system, in that database we would find every single citizen of the Republic of Serbia and information about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 411, we have several extracts from this uniform database, or unified database. Could you take a look at that, please, tab 411. There's several examples there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. It is the single database that exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here we have information about every citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me confirm this. We have one page translated, the first page. Is the reason the same as in the previous tab, this is illustrative of the others?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same. Just the names are different. And I'd like to ask the witness which information, what data we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this system, does the system contain data on all the citizens of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And here we can see from each of these examples the basic data, the kind of information. Of course, if additional information is needed, then that can be retrieved as well, with respect to ID cards, any weapons, weapons permits or things like that, driver's licences and so on. And here we can see the type of personal data that can be found in the database.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Small point, Your Honour: I know we normally try to display on the overhead projector, for those viewing, documents when we're going through a document-heavy part of the evidence. If there is a spare copy and if it could be done without delaying matters, it might make the evidence more intelligible to those viewing this publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll bear that in mind. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what this data contains. We have basic data, and then it says at the end: "Do you wish to continue investigation into this individual?" And then the search can continue. So what information does this contain?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first point is the personal registration number for each citizen, then the surname, the father's name, and the first name, place of birth, employment or profession, the blood type, the ID card, identification card, where it was issued, et cetera, and place of residence and when that place of residence was reported. So these are basic data on each individual. Plus the address. Yes, plus the address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then anything else you can go in to search and find other relevant information?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about this uniform database, let me ask you something not related to Izbica but to the database system itself. With the existence of this database system, would there be any sense in taking away personal documents at the border crossing to prevent Albanians leaving Yugoslavia to go back? This is another thing that has been bandied about in this room here and that was referred to by those who represent Mr. Nice's side.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be nonsensical to confiscate somebody's IDs and thereby prevent him going back to the country. There are daily instances in which people in third countries tend to lose their ID documents. This doesn't mean that they can't come become to the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just explain: Why would it be nonsensical to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be nonsensical, in my opinion, Your Honour President of this Trial Chamber, because all the citizens of the Republic of Serbia are recorded, in addition to other methods, in this general database system. So it would be inconceivable to believe that if we take away somebody's ID papers, that he -- that person would not be able to return to the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thanks very much. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was an Official Note compiled on the burial of the bodies found in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of Official Notes were compiled, as far as I remember, as many as there were places where the burial was conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just draw your attention to tab 408 where there is an Official Note that was compiled on the 7th of June, 1999, and we can see that it was the secretariat of Kosovska Mitrovica, and it is taken in order. It was compiled on the 7th of June by the official of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica with respect to the exhumation of 101 bodies on the 4th of June. Did that take place after all the investigation work was completed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says on the 4th of June we have one location, the bodies buried there, then another location on the 4th, and then on the 5th, et cetera. What does this second Official Note mean, the one that was done in Kraljevo subsequently by forensic workers?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please give a reference. Mr. Milosevic is reading very fast from something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the precise reference? The interpreters have asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking again about tab 408 that contains two Official Notes, one containing information about the location where all these bodies were buried, and the second one shows that the police always updates information and tries to find even the smallest error, if any, in order to correct it. So two years later, in this case number, it says Dibrani Djevdet. That's the name. The number 7 is registered properly in the document, and then it says in the last paragraph on page 2 of the subject document, instead of "An inscription was read at the grave site UCK Dibrani Djevdet," and so on and so forth, it should say "No inscription was found at the grave site and the search did not produce any documents." Is it proof that the police tried to correct errors and update information?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They always try to correct previous conclusions which do not correspond to the reality, and this is a reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They also mention some error with numbers. It says: "Bodies numbered 48 and 58 are listed in the previous note as disinterred from grave number 61." In regard to body number 48, it should say exhumed from grave site 41. In any case, the file isn't closed until the complete investigation has been finalised.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see. General, in all the places where exhumations were done, were there appropriate reports compiled with photo files?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we find them in tabs 412 to 416?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I hope there's no need to leaf through these tabs except to note that both the reports and photo documentation were compiled during exhumations.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to quote 66(g) again. I hope you still remember it because I quoted it several times. Let me ask you: Did you and other members of the Ministry of the Interior, when you were searching for Izbica and when you were taking these investigative and forensic steps and other measures, know about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time you were completely unaware of any indictment or any allegations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that for certain. Maybe we knew about the indictment, but we certainly didn't know about these specific allegations. We might have known about the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because this one was brought on the 24th of May. Did the search for Izbica begin by that time?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the search for Izbica begin before the 24th of May? That's the date of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it started a couple of days prior. I believe that page was found on the Internet and broadcast on some TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about this photograph, I'm asking you when the search for Izbica began; before the indictment or after?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, if the dates you gave me are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to look at the list of names in Schedule F? Did you see all of it? And do the names correspond with those in the indictment? Did you notice any discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already that I compared these two and that there are certain discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that was obtained during the previously described investigation, does it point to different conclusions than those stated in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information that we had, including the information we have in these tabs, point to a different course of event to the one described in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible for these deaths to occur during fighting between KLA forces and the security forces of our country?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is incontestable. First of all, we can see from the photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have exhausted Izbica. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to hear the end of this witness's answer to my previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. All the questions you have asked are leading, although I've allowed them. Mr. Milosevic, you present a novel experience for me in comparison with the jurisdiction in which I practice. One would go through an entire trial and not hear one objection on the basis of a leading question being asked, but here the Prosecutor is always on his feet because it is more the norm than the exception for you to ask leading questions, particularly in this phase of your examination where you are closing off. My ruling is that you must move to another area. You have exhausted Izbica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the suggestion of Mr. Robinson, dear General, we will move to another subject, which is also covered in the allegations made by Mr. Nice. Let me see which paragraph that is. It is about the Dubrava prison, 66(k). General, do you have any knowledge about the bombing of the Dubrava prison or about evacuation of prisoners or something similar?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you personally engaged in the events related to the bombing of the Dubrava prison by the NATO forces in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally engaged in the action of evacuation of prisoners from the Dubrava prison towards Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many inmates there were in the prison before the bombing?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than a thousand but less than 1.100, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a general idea what -- on what kind of charges these inmates were convicted, what kind of crimes they had committed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes of terrorism, illegal possession of weapons, and the criminal act of association for the purpose of engaging in hostile activities. Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have relevant exhibits in tabs 202 to 210. I will now ask you a series of questions about the basic facts concerning these events and then about your personal involvement. General, tell me, please, who was in charge of the security detail in the prison?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service of the prison itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean is that the service charged with the execution of sentences and all the accompanying services?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It belongs to the Ministry of Justice of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, how many projectiles were used in the NATO airstrike on the Dubrava prison?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the airstrikes went on for three days, off and on, from the 19th to the 22nd May 1999. And the prison was hit with several dozen projectiles, maybe over 50, 60, maybe even more, I'm not sure. But certainly not less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in tab 202, can we find one excerpt from the chronological report on these events compiled by the prison authorities? It goes date by date; 19th of May, 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this document, I hear the way it's been introduced as an excerpt from a chronological history. If that history relates generally to this topic, to have been provided with a selective excerpt might be unsatisfactory and it would be helpful to know if we are going to be provided with the full document. And again, with 400-odd documents to deal with in cross-examination that I hope will not exceed two days, I'm simply not going to be able to pick up all these points later on. So may we know whether this is an extract of a document that's going to be provided or made available to me in full?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a reasonable question, Mr. Milosevic. The chronological report to which reference is made, where is it? Will it be adduced as evidence here? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already received it. That is the complete chronological report that we have reviewed here. I believe it is still -- I don't know if we have it among the tabs for General Stevanovic, but we certainly had it among the exhibits presented through the chief of Secretariat of Internal Affairs for Pec, Mr. Paponjak. That was the report on all incidents involving loss of life. This is just an excerpt from the same document which you have a copy of in it's entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if it is already evidence here, then it should have a number. I see we are past the time for the break. Have that matter investigated during the break, Mr. Milosevic. Perhaps the Prosecutor can assist, and Mr. Kay. We'll take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we break, can I make one observation. Mr. Milosevic, we had enough, more than enough evidence on the bombing of NATO, on Dubrava prison. Speaking for myself, what I'd like to hear from the general is that what happened on 22nd and 23rd of May and the bodies with gunshot wounds. That's the critical evidence. Bear that in mind in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, according to the reports that you received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind the observations of Judge Kwon and concentrate on that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The witness is not receiving any interpretation. Yes. Are you now hearing? Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, bearing in mind Mr. Kwon's observation, do you know exactly when the Dubrava prison was targeted? Please look at tab 204. That contains information about NATO bombing of the Dubrava correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Is there any translation for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are no translations. I've inquired of the associate -- not -- Ms. Anoya, whether she knows when these documents are going to be available in translation because it's particularly important for me that I'm able to explore the Dubrava documents but at the moment they aren't available, but I shall certainly want to go through them in one format or another with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we have any information as to when the translations of these documents will be available? Does the court deputy have any information on this? Or do we have any information as to when they were submitted for translation? Mr. Milosevic, when were they submitted for translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a lot more than a month ago, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the information from the court deputy is that the documents were received by the ODM on the 19th of May, less than a week ago and not a month ago as you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not have any other information. There aren't any new documents ever since the general's been here, and he's been here for quite awhile now. All the documents have been submitted for translation. How records are kept of this is something that I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not certain what the Trial Chamber is to make of this procedure. Apparently the explanation may be that they were submitted more than a month ago in bulk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have something from the -- we have a statement from the court deputy which says that the documents received by the ODM on the 19th of May are the following tabs, and there are quite a number, and the one that we're looking at here, which is tab 20 -- 204 is among those received on the 19th of May. It is for you, Mr. Milosevic, in the light of this information, to explain to the Chamber why we should allow you to lead evidence on this document at all since it was only submitted a week ago. You are in charge of the management of your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the documents were handed over when I said they were. However, there is no doubt when the translation service is overburdened they return documents and then they again record the date when they take them back in as the date when they were originally admitted. They do not record the original date when they were first taken in, only the date when they were returned yet again after they were taken back. For the record, I wish to draw your attention to something that is obvious. Mr. Robinson, several times here you pointed out that I have a privileged position because they are translating 1.000 pages per month for me, which is not the case in any other trial. I would like to draw your attention to the following: That I received from Mr. Nice at least 600.000 pages, according to his records. If I were to have the equivalent number of pages to proffer, then according to this privileged position of mine, 600 months would be needed for the translation of all of that. That is to say 50 years. Therefore, you can only be guided by these comparative mathematics in order to draw this conclusion: That 1.000 pages per month is a privilege and how that is a constraint on the possibility of adducing evidence in any way. I would like to say to you that, for example, for witness Momir Bulatovic, the documents were handed over last year. Last week I was informed that half of them have not been translated yet. I respect the fact that the translation service is working at its own pace. They're working very hard, but within the scope of their possibilities. However, that certainly is not in line with the pace of presenting evidence, especially if we look at the amount of documents handed over to me by the other side, and especially when you compare this to the fact that an enormous number of these documents were not even translated into Serbian to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think what you say may be true, that you handed the documents in in bulk over a month ago. The Translation Unit would have returned some of those documents to you because of their workload. But what is not clear to me is why, if they returned documents to you and you knew that you would need this document for evidence at a particular time, why did you not ensure that that document was returned to the Translation Unit for translation in time for this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed that Professor Rakic, who is here now and who has been here for over a month, always made an effort to accommodate the translation service. He always tried to tell them what the priorities were. The extent of his success is limited by the scope of the translation service's possibilities, and things get out of his control and my control. This admission of documents and then returning them and so on and back and forth, that is something that is complicated, and on the other hand it's not in our hands. It's not in my hands or his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to make it clear that I see this matter quite differently. There is no evidence at the moment that satisfies me that any of the documents we're looking at were submitted in bulk and then returned by the ODM. But even allowing for that, even if that is correct, the question that has to be addressed is why the documents were submitted again, if it's again, for translation on the 19th of May and why you, as the person presenting the documents, cannot given us an explanation for that, why you're not able to say that they were returned to you and that they were again sent in for translation on the 19th of May. Instead of that, you create a smokescreen by referring to Bulatovic, which has got nothing to do with the issue at the moment. The issue at the moment relates exclusively to when these documents that you now seek to produce for Dubrava prison were submitted officially in the proper way for translation, and you failed to give any explanation of why that was on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents are resubmitted because they had been returned. Had they not been returned, they would not be resubmitted to begin with. I mentioned Mr. Bulatovic as an example of the great burden on the translation service. There is this limit, and that absolutely does not keep up with the pace of the evidence presented here and also the pace at which witnesses are called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question remains, Mr. Milosevic, why was this document, and a number of other documents, too, only resubmitted on the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably because that was when the translation service could admit them. They're on standby all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just assist. There is a thousand-page limit. There are a large number of documents that have been put forward for certain witnesses who are to come, such as Momir Bulatovic. That creates a pressure on the system. If they're working on those documents, they can't work on current documents. But those documents in relation to Bulatovic have to be presented in a timely fashion. Documents then get returned and they have to go back into the system in batches. A witness such as this will be covering a number of important items, but it goes in in batches, and unfortunately something like the Dubrava prison went in on the 19th of May batch. The problem is the capping procedure of 1.000 pages. So it is right it was submitted on the 19th of May, but it's a bit like hospital waiting lists in my own country which caused a difficulty. There may be a waiting list of only 48 hours, but it depends when you're allowed to book it. So the request went in some time ago, it being returned because of the 1.000 cap. It creates a problem on the numerous exhibits that he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what is not clear, Mr. Kay, is -- are you saying, then, that Mr. Milosevic has no control over when the document is submitted or resubmitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, he has no control. He's in the prison, so in fact it's actually done by people on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I know he has associates, I know that, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the court liaison. But the thousand pages is such a small amount in relation to this particular trial that it does create pressure in the reproduction of his documents as well as working on documents that are to be produced in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The fact is that the translation unit has been always working in its full capacity. The issue is the matter of priority. So the question is whether the accused could have done that kind of arrangement properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would have occurred this way: That if the Dubrava prison documents had not been translated, the Izbica documents would not have been translated. It really is quite -- quite circular in its manifestation in relation to this number of files. And no one's criticising the translation department. It is realised and the accused appreciates that they work very hard, it is the allocation of resources, and the point he makes is I bet the Prosecution are not subject to a thousand-page limitation each month, which is a fair observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They're not subject to a 1.000 page limitation every month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, all of these remarks are of some relevance to this issue, but it may be you've not seen this report and you should see it. It should be given to you. But it is interesting to note that among the documents submitted for translation in relation to this witness, there were 323 which had already been translated by the service, and of these 125 of them had already been translated for this case. So very little assistance is apparently given by the accused in identifying any priority in translation or even identifying documents which are essential. So there is an another side to this story, and it becomes even more important when you bear in mind the submissions you're making about the difficulties that face the translation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That does meet my sympathy and I do understand -- understand that, and I wouldn't try to make an argument in response to that in relation to documents that have already been translated, which is why they now have the screening process, so that people can track these documents. But they aren't the translation department. They are, of course, another department that has been set up as a screening process, and no one wants the waste of resources of things being translated twice. Finding where those copies of previously translated documents are, if they're not exhibits in this case already, is another matter. They may be with someone else's archives or papers in relation to the Prosecution, I don't know. But it is a problem. I was talking last week about it and wondered if the embassy from the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro could not assist here by supplying at least three support staff in relation to translation for Mr. Milosevic, that they be working here continuously.
