They would have people of sufficient linguistic ability, knowledge of English, to be able to input such resources into this Tribunal to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make two points, one built on the last and designed to be helpful, and the other a correction. The Prosecution was heavily dependent on the use of draft translations. Had it been necessary to have everything translated by CLSS, we wouldn't have reached the position we're in at all, it wouldn't have been possible. Of course there's an unevenness, sometimes, in the quality of translation but we can live with that. And the accused, knowing the problems that he was going to face, together with Mr. Kay could have and arguably should have considered at an earlier stage using draft translations. The Court may remember that at one stage in not only this case but another case made use of a university, Novi Sad, where certain categories of documents were put out for translation because of the burden of translation on this Court. The corrective point is this: When the accused seeks to compare the thousand page limit, if that is the limit for him as opposed to the limit for CLSS generally and for us and the material we produced to him, of course a very large part, probably at least half of the material produced to the accused by us, was material that could have been favourable to his case and that it was our duty to provide him in order to help him. He has no such duty do provide material to us and is only concerned with translating material positive to his case. I remain, of course, clearly of the position that this material is likely to be helpful to the Chamber and in particular may well be helpful to His Honour Judge Kwon's concerns because they are broadly contemporaneous documents, if they are what they appear to be, and I know that there's at least one or two of them that I wish to refer to. So my concern is only how we can get the material before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I notice that 204 is short, three pages. Perhaps that -- we could have that placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just one other thing. In the same as I was grateful to Ms. Dicklich for drawing our attention to the reality of our use of draft translators, it's only fair that I should also caution the -- caution -- alert the Chamber to the fact that tab 22, if you turn to it not now but perhaps later, would appear to be an example of CLSS being burdened twice with the production of the same document because there are two CLSS translations for the same document in tab 22, and that's not the only occasion that's been happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that was translated twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would appear so because there are two CLSS translations and it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the screening process failed. I believe that the Chamber has a duty to investigate this matter with the CLSS and also to investigate the possibility of the kind of help that Mr. Kay referred to. If that is possible, I think it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with the latter point, but I have to say I understood the matter had been investigated and we had the report in front of us and it's on the basis of that that I've been dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think in the light of all the information that is before the Trial Chamber, I would be reluctant to take any action that is inimical to the accused because the information is at this stage unclear in my view. I think what we have to do is place the document on the ELMO. It's relatively short and the interpreters would be able to offer a translation of those parts of the document, Mr. Milosevic, which are important and relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. But before I place the document on the overhead projector, I should like to ask you to clear up one point about the return of documents. I really don't have the time to go into this question of sending out and taking back the documents. I assume that if I have tendered documents and received documents that are to be tendered I think that I've done the job. I can't go back and select documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. I want to make this position quite clear: The documents may be returned to you once you send them in bulk, but you have an obligation then to identify to the CLSS on a priority basis those documents that you will need for a particular witness. So it is not enough for you to say you send all the documents in. Once they're returned to you, you must then identify for the CLSS those that you need to be translated on a priority basis, because you know when your witnesses are coming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, well, I don't send out documents that I don't need the translation of. So if something is linked to the testimony of General Stevanovic, for example, then it goes without saying that once the documents were handed over, then they will be used during his testimony, and we know exactly when he's going to testify. So Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there are no documents that I sent in that need not be translated. So I don't know what this priority refers to, then, whether they're going to use one part of the documents -- or we're going to use one part of the documents one day and another part the next day. That doesn't change anything; they have to be translated, and there's no danger of them being translated twice. And what Mr. Bonomy said, that there were a lot of documents translated, that is quite true, because translated documents mostly refer to Racak in this part of the case, but they weren't translated twice nor were they sent in for translation twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, Mr. Milosevic, you're on notice that it's up to you to justify the introduction of untranslated documents and therefore you will have to have an explanation. It's for you to record whether documents have been returned to you, whether life has been made difficult for you by the CLSS. It's not for us to investigate that. And if you fail to satisfy me, then my inclination may be to refuse to consider the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, for this particular document we'll proceed as I indicated. Let it be placed on the ELMO. That's 204.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see page 2, not to waste time. It's a brief document, piece of information about the bombing, a report on the bombing. And it is linked to Mr. Kwon's question earlier on. He said he was interested exclusively in the 22nd of May, because here we have listed all the instances of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4 on page 2 of this document, and it's a very brief paragraph, could you read what it says, General, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 page 2, you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "NATO bombing was repeated from 1700 hours to 1805 hours and then again at 2310 hours, and on the 22nd of May, 1999, at 0610 hours. A total of 48 air bombs were launched." That is paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that part of the information refers to the 22nd of May and the bombing that took place on the 22nd of May. Now, do you know what facilities within the prison were hit during the bombing when Dubrava prison was bombed from the 19th to the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the facilities were hit of the prison, all the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be helpful if, even at this stage, answers to general questions of that kind which bring forth answers "As far as I know..." are qualified so that we know what is the source of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a point that you make generally, Mr. Nice. It's of course open to you in cross-examination to test the witness on those matters. But let us hear, General, what is the source of this information that you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My source were the officials in the SUP of Pec through which I was interested in knowing, learning about the consequences of the bombing because I was in the SUP of Pristina or rather, the MUP headquarters there. So it was logical for me to want to be informed about that because the bombing was frequent with a lot of projectiles dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, since you yourself were at the MUP headquarters, did you receive information about all the bombings in Kosovo and Metohija that took place from the police authorities depending on whose territory the bombing took place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the MUP of Pristina received daily reports from all the SUP offices about each specific bombing that they were able to identify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through that information did you also receive information that all the buildings of the Dubrava prison were bombed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of that information, and when I personally asked, I was given oral information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how many persons were killed in those attacks, and how many prisoners were there among them?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100 persons were killed, perhaps give or take two, plus or minus two, and I think that most of those people were prisoners, with the exception of one individual, and he was the deputy warden of the prison who also lost his life in one of those bombings, I think the second or third instance of bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many people were wounded?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little less than 200 persons were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us when and who issued the order about the deployment of the police in order to evacuate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally conveyed by telephone the order from the minister that pursuant to a request from the Ministry of Justice that they give assistance to the evacuation of the prisoners, but the head of the staff of the headquarters, I think on the 23rd, sent out an order ordering the SUP of Pec to give their assistance to the officials of the prison in Dubrava and transfer them to Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at tab 207, please. Tab 207 contains a dispatch, a telegram. The number is 132. It is from the staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in Pristina. The number of the dispatch is 132 and it's dated the 23rd of May, 1999, to the head of SUP Pec, and then it says: "On the 24th of May, 1999, in Istok, at the latest by 9.00, to organise the evacuation of all the prisoners in the -- to the Lipjan prison facility with maximum security measures to be observed. And if the need arises, to have buses secure the location for an investigation," and it is signed by the official of the MUP staff. And then -- so that is the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question? You're not giving the evidence, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is -- I quoted the document, it is a photocopy of the dispatch. The question was who issued the order to engage the police in the evacuation process? And the general explained to us that it was issued by the staff of the -- or headquarters of the SUP of Pec and this proves -- tab 207 proves that that is correct, where we can see the order in dispatch form issued to the Pec SUP. Now, General, when did the evacuation actually take place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation took place as planned on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, can I ask you, before or at the time of the evacuation were prisoners -- were a number of prisoners shot in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean before the evacuation or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Either that or during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely have no knowledge of any fact of that kind nor do I know about anything of the kind now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence is you've no information that any prisoner at Dubrava prison in the course of the latter half of May was shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you follow the evidence of Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I was not able to because I was prohibited from doing so because I was waiting to testify myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear about the escape attempt of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I did have some information that that -- that the possibility of an escape was there, but I didn't actually hear that the escape actually was attempted, that it took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Picking up on this question raised by Mr. Bonomy as to whether anybody was shot, whether anybody was killed at the prison, I have here two sheets from the exhibits of Mr. Nice. One has the ERN number of 03030802, and the last numbers of the other one are 0807. These are reports by the Spanish forensic team tendered by the other side. If they are available, they could be put on the overhead projector, but I have only one copy. There is a stamp, Ministry of Justice Forensics Institute, Cartagena: "[In English] -- the organs that are already decomposing, and this cause would be shock wave." "... we must find the cause of death that would act upon the organs that are already decomposing, and this cause would be shock wave."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read this first in order to ask the question, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Working Hypothesis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness says he has no information about anyone being shot. That's the end of the matter as far as he's concerned. There's no point in putting forensic material to him since he knows nothing of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, it says here in exhibit under the number I gave, very clearly: "At this moment the rest of the deaths [In English] would have occurred as a result of use of short and long firearm, grenades, et cetera, in order to suppress the massive escape."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I repeat, the witness knows nothing about an escape attempt, therefore there's no point in asking him about it. This is a stage for questions, not for submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the general is qualified to answer my question. He said that he is not aware that anybody was killed attempting to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question, General, is this: If somebody had been killed attempting to escape, would that have qualified as a murder or would that have been a legal use of firearm? Do you have any evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- don't answer that question. It's an improper the question. The witness can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice very frequently asks hypothetical questions of a much more general character than this question of mine. So the Spanish claim that somebody was killed trying to escape. I'm just asking if somebody had, would that have been a legitimate use of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have ruled. I am not allowing the witness to answer a question as to whether in his view a certain action would have qualified -- would qualify as murder. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't what hear anything more about it. Just move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just for the record, I didn't ask the witness's opinion. I'm just asking him what the regulations stipulate in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're beginning to test my patience. Either you have a proper question to ask or we'll stop the examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what forensic examinations have been performed in relation to the dead in Dubrava, and who ordered such examination?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the investigative judge of the district court in Pec. What was done was to compile the forensic examination reports, external examination of the bodies was performed. Upon orders of the investigating judge, the competent police authorities participated in the burial of bodies and the compiling of the criminal investigation and forensic reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this incident in Dubrava treated as a secret? Was the investigation confidential or was it open to the public?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no secret. All the materials are to be found in these binders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, during the performance of the on-site investigation was the press present on many occasions in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the press was present at least once, possibly on more occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, after the arrival of the KFOR and UNMIK in Kosovo was it at all possible for our authorities to continue their investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further investigation by our authorities was practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I emphasise, Mr. Robinson, that in tabs from 202 until 213 we can find the documents related to Dubrava so that -- let me just take a moment. No, I can't find -- yes. It's in 202 until 210. I'm not going to dwell on that any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in the indictment there is reference to Suva Reka as well. What information do you have regarding any incidents involving loss of life in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, there were incidents in Suva Reka involving loss of life, and in our materials here two such incidents are cited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do these cases concerning Suva Reka exist in tabs 214 until 259?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They begin with 214, and the last one is 234.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 234, then. Now, nothing is to be found here, or maybe I cannot find any point of contact regarding police action concerning Suva Reka incidents. Is it the case that some of these incidents relate in any way to 66(d), which says that: "On or about 26th of March, 1999, in the morning hours, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the vicinity of the Berisha family compound in town of Suva Reka." Then the same claims are made, that people were separated, arrested, et cetera. Does anything to be found in these tabs relate to Suva Reka incidents?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to find -- in fact, I tried to compare the allegations made in the indictment with what we know about Suva Reka incidents, and I found nothing in common except that both refer to Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to have a large number of documents concerning Suva Reka. How can it be possible that none deal with what is described in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the police had known anything that might match the allegation in the indictment, an investigation would have been performed and report made. This incident from the indictment involves a much larger number of victims, and it is simply impossible that it would have been overlooked. And we have a lot of documents, indeed, ending with tab 259. One batch ends with tab 234, and the other batch ends with 259.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us assume that this event really happened. I believe we even heard testimony to that effect. Do you have an explanation as to how it was possible for the police not to be informed about this event? How come they never learned about it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many impossible explanations. It could have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That sounds like speculation. We are in the curious position that apparently the accused and/or the witness and/or the accused's associates have put together a considerable quantity of material that may be contemporaneous and therefore may -- or comparatively contemporaneous, and that therefore may be of interest to the Chamber for what it reveals. Sadly, either little or none of it is translated, and so as opposed to the Chamber having the assistance of this material - and at the moment I don't know how much assistance I'm going to derive from it - it's being asked to listen to mere speculation from the witness. It doesn't seem to me very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I will not allow the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson. Then I won't deal with Suva Reka any more. But I hope it is obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... report? Is there a police report, General, on the investigations which they carried out in relation to Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presiding Judge, in these several dozen tabs that I named, there is evidence about police investigation about these two incidents in which the total number of victims was 17. A complete police report is available, and most of the bodies were identified. We can see those documents starting with tab 215, ending with the tabs I already mentioned. But I already said it is difficult to link these two cases with the incident alleged in the indictment. There is not a single surname of Berisha among the identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the police investigated a different incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police investigated the incident that it was informed about; in fact, two incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not clear to me where your evidence is leading. If you have specific information on the basis of police reports which contradict or attempt to contradict the evidence in 66(d), then that is what you should be putting forward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, all these tabs dealing with Suva Reka represent evidence that the police investigated every incident known to them, and the general explained that the only cases they didn't investigate were the ones they didn't know about. There is not a single reason to conclude that the police had any ulterior motives to investigate one incident but not to investigate another. The only possible reason was that they didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you have concluded adducing evidence on Suva Reka, then proceed to the next area of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only rise to make perhaps an obvious point but it's a problem that obviously concerns us. If this material has nothing to do with the allegations, then it should simply be excluded because it's irrelevant, or could be excluded because it's irrelevant. But if on finally being provided in translation the accused wishes to raise some argument that the content of this material actually goes actively to disprove our case but by then the witness is gone, it will have been impossible properly to cross-examine on the material and to make what might, for all I know, very valuable points for the Prosecution arising from it. I'm in this dilemma: If I seek to exclude the material, which would be to take a candidly adversarial approach, I may be denying either ourselves the opportunity to have material that could be of value. I may, more significantly, be denying the Chamber the benefit that it might find in its search for proof or truth from this material. It really Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is extremely unsatisfactory that this material is not translated and that the accused takes no regard of the Court's observations about translation and just brushes it aside. It's as if he'd -- it's as if he disregards altogether the very difficult task that the Chamber is doing and that it can do most effectively on the basis of material that is contemporaneous when it exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to determine how you present your case. If you're seeking to rely on any of these untranslated documents, if the document is relatively short we can have it placed on the ELMO. If you believe it is relevant and helpful to your case it may be placed on the ELMO and the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 19 it says: "A superior is responsible for the criminal acts of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that -- if he knew or had reason to know that they were about to commit such acts or had done so, and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators." We have here an act regarding Suva Reka, and you told us about the information you had, and you explained that all the cases, all the incidents that the police knew about were investigated. Could it have happened that the police knew about something without starting an investigation and without taking measures to prevent it or to punish perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can't allow that question, Mr. Milosevic. It's inviting speculation. What you can do in relation to Article 7(3) is to adduce evidence that shows that the police carried out investigations. You have been doing that. It's then for the Chamber to determine whether the ingredients in paragraph 19 have been substantiated. You can't ask the witness to speculate in the manner that you have been doing. You have to adduce the evidence. Adduce the evidence which in your view supports your case, and we will make a decision on the basis of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, evidence here is that the police did investigate what they knew about. The general is explaining that what is contained in this indictment is something that the police could not have investigated because they simply did not know about it. The evidence here shows that the police acted in accordance with the law concerning matters that they were aware of. How could they act in accordance with the law about something that they had no idea about? I cannot prove --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's your case. That's your case. And perhaps the Chamber will agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very hard to prove that the police did not know something that they did know. I mean, how can someone prove that he didn't know something that he didn't know? There is evidence that the police investigated what they knew about, so isn't it logical to assume that had they known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is not the time for speeches. Proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will continue to deal with the accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, 66(l)(i) pertains to Kotlina. (l)(i), it has to do with Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what it says here: "On or about the 24th of March, 1999, the village of Kotlina was attacked by forces of the FRY and Serbia. In the course of the attack, most of the houses were burnt down and at least 17 persons were killed. Some of those killed were captured in the woods, executed, and then thrown into wells. Explosives were thrown on top of the wells." General, do you have any knowledge of what happened in the village of Kotlina near Kacanik on the 24th of March, 1999, when a few persons lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the basis for the knowledge that he has.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I see the transcript -- I should correct that. What I said was, "And the basis for the knowledge that he has."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this knowledge from my conversations with the then head of the SUP in Urosevac and also from the insight I had in the case file established by the Urosevac SUP concerning matters that they did know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I read out to you a description of events that is contained in this paragraph 66(l)(i). Does this description of events correspond with what you know of what had happened in the village of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This description from the indictment does not correspond to my knowledge and does not correspond to the facts of that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the core of the case from Kotlina on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event in Kotlina can be described as a conflict between the police and army on the one hand and a terrorist group from Kotlina on the other. It occurred while the terrain was being searched. This was being carried out in accordance with the plan of the border units of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. In tabs 211, 12, and 213, are there documents of the Ministry of the Interior related to Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or, rather, not about events in the plural but about the event in Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the three tabs concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you're going to ask him about 211, let it be placed on the ELMO. We have a translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand we just received translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please explain first what kind of documents these are. I'm talking about tabs 211, 212, and 213.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 211, we have a document of -- that is sent to the judge of the municipal court in Urosevac, and attached thereto is photo documentation of the on-site investigation. It is an integral part of the on-site investigation record. That is tab 211.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when was the on-site investigation carried out?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The on-site investigation report is not contained here, as far as I can see, but this document shows that it was carried out on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who carried out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document also shows that the investigating judge of the municipal court in Urosevac, Ljiljana Milicevic -- or Ljilja Milicevic, carried out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of the SUP of Urosevac take part in the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the on-site investigation completed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was only a partial investigation carried out?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A partial investigation was carried out due to security reasons, because obviously there was a danger from attacks by terrorist groups. This can be seen from tab 213 in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say when -- when was the on-site investigation carried out; the same day, the 24th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same day. That fact can be seen from the date of this document contained in tab 211, because the technical documents are provided on the 24th and the event concerned obviously took place on the 24th, so the on-site investigation obviously took place on the 24th too. That can also be seen from tab 212, the date of the report of the forensic examination of the scene. That document also bears the date of the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you just mentioned the document in tab 212. This is a report on forensic examination of the scene.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how was the event described?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was described as terrorism. That could be seen from paragraph one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of steps were taken? What does it say here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph five it says the scene was examined in detail, photographed and filmed, traces of items were found, and that is what can be seen here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we are going to have a look -- or, rather, can we see from this why the MUP unit came to Kotlina on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their objective was to search the area in the border belt, according to the plans of the group of the army of Yugoslavia in charge of border control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is Kotlina from the state border?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what the distance is, but I'm sure that it is in the border area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area of providing security for the state border.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in-depth security of the state border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this action of providing this kind of security did members of the army take part in it as well?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the on-site investigation, what was done with the corpses of the persons who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the corpses were not gathered or transported. They remained on site. And according to this document, we are not aware of what happened to the corpses subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain what can be seen from the photographs from the site itself. As for this event in Kotlina an on-site investigation was carried out, photographs were taken, and they are contained in tab 212.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest, gentlemen, that these photographs be placed on the ELMO so that everyone can see them. I'm going to ask the general to explain each and every individual photograph or, rather, what can be seen on each and every individual photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we see these pictures, can you find the names in this document of those who appear in the indictment, Schedule L?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- or, rather, we can ask the general, but I think they weren't identified then at all and an on-site investigation was carried out in terms of what had happened. The date matches fully. And the event occurred, and there is a report on the on-site investigation and examination and on the scene itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. The identification of corpses obviously had not been carried out due to security concerns, because the corpses remained on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that the on-site investigation had not been completed.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason why it had not been brought to an end?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the 24th of March. This is Kotlina. And these are the allegations contained in the indictment that I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on the security reasons? I don't follow that. And I don't understand why the people were not aware of the -- what happened with the corpses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I mentioned security reasons during my testimony, this primarily refers to the danger of being attacked by terrorist groups. Obviously here when it is said security reasons, that is the kind of danger that was meant. That could certainly be seen better from the on-site record of the investigating judge. Regrettably, it is not contained in these documents and probably -- it's probably in the investigation files. The investigating judge carries out the on-site investigation and he or she is the one who decides whether it has to be interrupted at a point and then mentions in his or her report the reasons why it had to be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can we now please have a look at these photographs. In the photographs that can be seen here, on the first page that was presented here in this collection of photographs -- could you please place that first page on the overhead projector. These are photographs 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every one of them has a caption too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you something in relation to what was established in the quotation that I read out to you from the indictment. These photographs 1, 2 and 3 show a few houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, houses can be seen, but whether it's a few, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, at least four can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the background, and then there's one here.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several houses can be seen. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you see a burned house on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot see a burnt house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On photograph number 1, does it say, "A broad view of the house where, according to the equipment found, the headquarters of the KLA were probably there"? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what's written in the caption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the second one, a close-up of the house where the KLA headquarters most probably were for the village of Kotlina. And then the next caption reads -- I can't read it. It's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably equipment and arms. I think that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the indictment that I quoted to you, is this logical that most houses were burned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not "is it logical," Mr. Milosevic. You can't ask him whether it's logical. Mr. Milosevic, do you have witnesses whom you will be calling in relation to these specific incidents who are closer to the incidents than the general? I ask that question because in my view the general is too far removed from the incidents to be very helpful to your case, and if you have witnesses who are closer to the incidents - for example, the persons who carried out the investigations - that would be much more helpful to your case. But it seems to me the general is very far removed. But it's a matter for you. For example, the allegation in the indictment that some of those killed were captured, executed and thrown into wells, if we had evidence -- if we had somebody who could tell us as to whether there were any wells on the site.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this documentation from the on-site investigation refutes the allegations made in the indictment, definitely so. First of all, we can see that these houses were not burnt down. That's the first point. Secondly, we'll come to the wells. They weren't wells at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's come to it after the break. It's now time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were discussing paragraph 66(l)(i) about the fact that during the attack or -- houses were allegedly burnt down. And Kotlina is also mentioned in another paragraph, that is to say in paragraph 63 of the indictment, (k)(i). So paragraph 63(k)(i) says on the 8th of March -- on or about the 8th of March, attacked and partially burnt the village of Kotlina. On then on the 24th of March, attacked again with heavy weapon systems, et cetera, et cetera. And it says at the end, not to have to read through everything it says, but it says: "Before departing Kotlina, forces of the FRY and Serbia burned the remainder of the village." So what is alleged here is not that most of the houses but the remainder of the village was also burnt, which to all intents and purposes means practically every house was burnt down. And here we see photographs taken on the 24th of March, the investigation on that day, where we can see houses without any traces of burning at all. So does this in any way be brought in connection with the correct, alleged assertions in the indictment? Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how was it concluded that in the house that appears on most of these photographs, which was filmed from the outside -- photographed from the outside and the inside, on what basis do you conclude that the KLA had its headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously that conclusion was made by the equipment and weapons that were found in that particular house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was there of equipment, ammunition and weapons on the 24th of March in the village of Kotlina? And I'd like to draw your attention to tab 212, which provides a list of the weapons and ammunition and equipment found on the 24th of March in Kotlina, Kacanik municipality. Here we have 31 things that are listed, 31 items or groups of items.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to find that list. Probably at the end of the photograph section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. At the end of the photograph section there's one more page, and what does it say? What was found there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says equipment and weapons described from numbers 1 to 31 inclusive, and it begins with sleeping bags, nine items or nine pieces; soldiers' bags, nine pieces; green rubberized trousers, et cetera; overalls, three; then 26, we have Chinese produced bombs; sanitary material, 20 pieces of that; semi-automatic rifles, eight pieces, made in China again, with ten rounds of ammunition. 29, the Stajer rifle, M-95; and 30 and 31 is ammunition, 7.62 millimetres for 224 clips, and ammunition 7.62 for an automatic rifle, 2.347 pieces of those. Now, does that list match the photographs ranging from 4 to 10 and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 21 to 24?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an attachment to the set of photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of tab 212, in the explanation that is given of the report on forensic examination of the scene and in noting what was observed and what is to be found on the photographs, what is shown on the photographs --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- it says, and that is at the beginning of the first third of the list on page 1 after the title page, it says bodies found in -- "View of bodies found overlooking the village of Kotlina in the immediate vicinity of a shelter in a well." So this mentions shelter and well. And then views of bodies found overlooking the village in Kotlina, one of the bodies photographed in the immediate vicinity of the well, and then second near another shelter which was in the form of a well. Now, why according to these documents, were most of the dead -- did most of the dead bodies appear on photographs 11 to 17, and why are they in the close vicinity of a hole which was shaped like a well?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably because the hole was used as a shelter. And according to the information that I received from the head of SUP Urosevac - and he received that information from people who went on site - it was absolutely -- there was no question of wells. There were just two holes, and they were connected by a tunnel, underground tunnel, and used as shelters for protection and shelter against any possible firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did the SUP get its information, this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SUP received that information on the basis of these photographs and also on the basis of the fact that the SUP employees took part in the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Milosevic, this bears out the point I made prior to the break, that the general is very far removed from this. If you had as a witness somebody who went to the site and who could speak to the shape of this hole and whether it was a well or not, that would be much more helpful. Of course we take in hearsay evidence here, but if you have better evidence than can be provided by the general, then you should provide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the event that the accused continues to rely on these photographs, they're not entirely clear in black and white and if there are any better versions, so I can understand exactly what they depict. They're not entirely clear as they appear in black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's perfectly true. Would you have any better versions, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Picture number 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any better photographs. These come from the on-site documentation, and these are photocopies of the original photographs taken then. Now, as far as the assertion goes of whether it was a well or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The general has a better version. Could you place picture -- pictures 19 and 20 on the ELMO, please. Yes, that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is on top is the hole, or well. What is at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read that part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photograph 20, it says under it: "A close-up of the second shelter described in the form of a well." So the upper one probably is the first well or first shelter in the form of a well, and the second one is the second shelter in the form of a well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this picture was taken from the top, from above. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The one we see in the second picture there is a ladder to climb up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on this photograph, the one mentioned a moment ago by Mr. Kwon, can you see some ladders on a completely dry bed of this well-shaped structure?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no water there, is there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the documents themselves, in the documentation from the on-site investigation carried out, it already says that it is -- we're dealing with shelters in the form of wells.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says, because a well would imply the existence of water, at least a minimum quantity of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, next to those bodies were there any weapons that were found that those people used in the clash between the -- them and the army and police? And I'd like to draw your attention to photographs 17 and 18 in that regard. What does it say underneath photograph 17 and 18?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under photograph 17, it says: "A close-up of the bodies found with the weapons and equipment which the people had with them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And photograph 16, what do we see there? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A view of the bodies found above the village of Kotlina in the close vicinity of the second shelter in the form of a well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the proposition that a well must always have water at the bottom is not borne out by empirical evidence. There are some parts of the world where wells are dry for a large part of the year. Even rivers may be dry. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in this documentation of the on-site investigation, these holes which it is stated were joined by tunnels and they were qualified as shelters or wells --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says they were shelters in the form of a well. So the well is a description of the shape of the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, can you comment what I just read out a moment ago? Let me repeat: Some of the persons killed were caught in the forest, killed and thrown into wells, and that explosives were thrown in later on; the wording in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that at all, and these photographs indicate bodies. You can see corpses that have not been thrown into a well. And of course it is difficult to assert this, but we can say that we -- no such traces can be seen in this well shape, and these photographs were taken on the 24th. It would be normal after the clash and not before the clash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we have any doubt that the photographs were taken after the clash?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. There can be no doubt on that score.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, now recently we heard testimony here by a SUP employee of Urosevac, Dragan Jasovic, who on the 10th of March, 1999, took a statement from an Albanian by the name of Becir Shefqet, and I have that statement here with me. Do you know of this statement by Becir Shefqet?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have the reference to the tab?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The reference, Mr. Milosevic, to the tab?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D295, tab 148. And you have the translation in front of you. 159 is the tab number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 138. We received a courtesy copy again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't received a courtesy copy. It may be duplicated in the tabs of this witness. If the accused could identify which one it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon. Mr. Kwon, I'm afraid that perhaps what I said wasn't translated properly. It is D295 of tab 158. The tab number is 158, not 138. 158 or 1.58 tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this statement, which was taken on the 10th of March, which would make it two weeks before the event in Kotlina took place allegedly, at the end of paragraph 2 it says the main headquarters of the KLA in the village of Ivaja, 380 members and substaffs of the KLA found in the village of Kotlina and the village of Pustenik of the Kacanik municipality. And then from the beginning of the last paragraph in his statement, it says the following: "The substaff of the KLA in the village of Kotlina," I don't know which building it was housed in, all I know is that the commander was Selim Kuci from Kotlina, and his deputy Miljanin Kuci from the same village. And the substaff of the KLA in Kotlina was where the main health infirmary was with Sevedin Kuci [phoen], and Fatin Loku [phoen], doctors both from the village of Kotlina. They worked there. The substaff of the KLA in the village of Kotlina numbered 150 members of the KLA. And then on page 2 it says, in the penultimate paragraph, that in the village of Ivaja, it says who was with him, and then it says Miljaim Loku from Kotlina. Miljaim Loku from Kotlina is mentioned, and Sali Bajram Vlashi too from Kotlina. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these two individuals, are they to be found in Schedule L, which enumerates the persons killed in Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please. Could the witness's microphone be switched on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I'd like to draw your attention to Schedule L, which contains the name of Miljaim Loku and Sali Vlashi, who according to the statement given by Shefqet Becir on the 10th of March, 1999, were members of the KLA precisely in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] I seem to be receiving the English interpretation on the B/C/S channel, and the B/C/S channel is number 6. There must have been a technical error there. But as I was saying, our state organs, regardless of the fact that we're dealing here with a clash between our forces and the KLA, after that event, did they take all steps provided for by the law which are generally taken in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The steps were taken as were possible, given the prevailing circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see those steps, those measures very clearly in this case file which contains the report of the on-site investigation in Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see them in this case file, but we could see them even more clearly if we had the on-site investigation report drawn up by the investigating judge of the district court in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness has made my point: Better evidence would come from the investigating report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't know if I really need to take the time to explain that, but this on-site investigation report and the photographs are not hearsay. They're all dated 24th of March. I suppose it casts a grave doubt indeed on the allegations made by Mr. Nice in the relevant paragraphs. I really don't know what other evidence you may require if this is not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us look at the Official Note in tab 213. That is from SUP of Urosevac. They made an Official Note concerning the incidents in Kotlina, again as part of a review of all incidents, because it was made in 2003.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is written in this Official Note drawn up by SUP Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for conducting the search of the terrain is stated. It also states that a special police unit from SUP Urosevac took part. I already said that a field search was conducted on the orders of the group for the in-depth security of state borders of the Yugoslav army. Combat activity occurred between the police and Yugoslav army on the one hand and KLA terrorists on the other, and according to unverified information, 22 unidentified terrorists who were active in the vicinity of the village of Kotlina were killed. We see again the same formulation; namely, for reasons of security, only a partial investigation was conducted by the investigating judge of the municipal -- of the district court, rather, Ljiljana Milicevic, including a whole team, including the prosecutor and the team of the Urosevac SUP. A criminal investigation and forensic reports have been created. Further treatment of the bodies and place and manner of burial are unknown. This is case number 73/03, dated 6 June 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the reasons for conducting this field search, what is written here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says following frequent -- increasingly frequent terrorist attacks on the road Urosevac-Kacanik-Djeneral Jankovic, which passes through the Kacanik gorge. So these increasingly frequent terrorist attacks were the reason.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And here we have an Official Note reflecting this.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm expecting this witness's examination to be concluded today. This is in keeping with your own projection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. I'm afraid, however, it won't be possible. Kindly point out any irrelevant matter that I may raise, because I'm really not intent on wasting time here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just gone over tab 213 for the second time. It was a pointless exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret, Mr. Bonomy, if I went through tab 213 for the second time. I did not have that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question: Do you have any information at all about the incident alleged in the indictment where in the village of Padaliste, Istok municipality, that is subitem (f), it says on the 26th of March, forces of Serbia and the FRY attacked Padaliste village, and entering the village, they shot at houses and locals who attempted to flee. So it is alleged that the forces entered the village and fired on villagers who attempted to flee.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that incident, but through a combination of circumstances I know that it is not in the Istok municipality but in Srbica municipality, and it has 700 to 800 locals, about 100 households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is so, would you have any explanation for the fact that exclusively members of one family were killed, all with the same surname? If Serbian and Yugoslav forces entered a village and fired on houses and villagers, how is it possible that only members of one family were killed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I have no information about that, but this description of events sounds unlogical bearing in mind the facts I've just stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the police knew nothing about this event.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It did not have any information about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move, and for my assistance, I'd be grateful if either the Court or the accused or the witness can identify the -- going back to Kotlina, could identify the second of the two names from D295, tab 1.58 that are on Schedule L. I've been able to identify one, which was Miljaim Loku, but of course the LiveNote transcript doesn't always pick up names at this stage, and I would be assisted if I could learn what's the second name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other one was Sali Vlashi, which was the last one. And this came from the evidence of Jasovic. This is all repetitive evidence from a previous witness who already covered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear anything. Can you get the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the full name we find in this Becir Shefqet statement is Selim Bajram Vlashi, and it's on the list of those killed. Sali Vllasi, that is what is written. So therefore neither in connection with the Padaliste village or in relation to other incidents alleged here there was no investigation, you say, for the reason that the police had no information about them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, please tell me one thing: According to the rules of your jurisdiction, or the jurisdiction applied here, how is one to prove negative facts such as that somebody didn't know something? How can you prove that the superior didn't know about something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... taken up now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked about this in relation to General Stevanovic's testimony, because he has information about all the incidents in Kosovo and Metohija and spent a long time there, and he's testifying that not a single criminal act went uninvestigated or unpunished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may very well have satisfied -- you may very well satisfy us that the charge is not proven so far as 7(3) is concerned. You have been adducing evidence as to the propriety of the conduct of the police, that they follow a system, they carry out investigations when they get reports. It's for us to draw certain conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us then go through a couple of more questions. You said that in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija the police registered over 1.500 incidents involving loss of life that are not encompassed by this indictment.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why is this fact important?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fact is important, first of all, because it shows that there is no reason whatsoever for the police to act differently in regard to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. incidents cited in the indictment if they had information about them. There is really no reason why we would have not acted upon the Berisha incident in Suva Reka had we known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did act in 1.500 cases, and you acted strictly in conformity with the regulations, and you didn't take action in the case of several incidents quoted here because you didn't know about them.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how did the police act --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to ascertain whether the 1.500 cases had any bearing upon the charges in the indictment. Can you speak to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the fact that action was taken in 1.500 cases confirms my claim that the police did act in all incidents that it knew about, and acted in keeping with the law. It bears no logical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Closing argument, not now. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how did the police act -- and other state authorities, for that matter; how did they act in incidents involving deaths?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way as they acted in the case of Izbica and in every other case that I have so far explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you brought here as an example, as an illustration, a number of documents relating to Pusto Selo. Can you describe the application of these procedures in a specific case, for instance, the case of Pusto Selo? How did the police find out about the mass graves in Pusto Selo near Orahovac, and what action did it take?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really a good illustration, but first let me deal with these tabs. But in addition to that case there is a number of other cases, especially where perpetrators of crimes are policemen, soldiers or reserve policemen, and they are under this tab. Speaking of Pusto Selo, we have had occasion in this session to see an aerial photograph, a satellite photograph of an alleged mass grave, and that is tab 420. Below this picture it says "Alleged mass grave." So somebody brought this photo to the headquarters with a caption "Alleged mass grave." Below this we see something written - I believe this is my handwriting - "This needs to be checked out urgently."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, General. You are very meticulous in your formulations. Do you think or do you know that it is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you write there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This needs to be checked out urgently. Go on the site, conduct as required an on-site investigation and take all the necessary measures." And the second bullet is: "Clean up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now explain: All of this regarding Pusto Selo is in tabs 419 to 433.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you got this information from the satellite, basically?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your first reaction was to have it verified. So what is to be seen in these tabs 419 to 433? What did you establish?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see the sequence of steps taken by the police in concert with all the other competent authorities, such as the judiciary. We see in 421 that an Official Note was drawn up and submitted to the district prosecutor. In 422, we see that on the basis of that Official Note the district prosecutor's office issues orders to the SUP in Prizren to gather additional information. Also, in tab 423, the district public prosecutor submits to the district investigating judge an exhumation -- sorry, submits a letter asking for an exhumation order to be made. And we can see this exhumation order under 424. Furthermore, we have two supplements to this exhumation order. In 425, we can see that the district prosecutor's office and the Secretariat of the Interior in Prizren received a report on the exhumation conducted in Pusto Selo. In the attachment, we see that 96 bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what paragraph in the indictment does this evidence relate?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It relates to the general conduct of the police. We took one specific example. You had the example of Izbica, which is in the indictment. You have Pusto Selo, which is not in the indictment, but in terms of its effects it is basically identical. The General has been saying that there are 93 casualties there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 96.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 96. What kind of action is taken and how the procedure evolves, the procedure conducted by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We -- I'll allow the evidence even though Pusto Selo is not in the indictment since that you're seeking to establish that there was a culture of proper conduct in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please. We really have to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want you to spend a lot of time on it. You have adduced the evidence in relation to Pusto Selo, which is not in the indictment. I've identified how it might be relevant and helpful to your case. Move on. Don't dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we're not going to dwell on Pusto Selo any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the entire course of the procedure applied is from tab 419 to 433; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other examples? You yourself, do you know of any other examples where you familiarised yourself with matters, where you actively participated in the resolution of issues?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give a few examples of victims who were civilians and perpetrators belonging to different categories of persons. I can give a few cases of that kind. The first case is the killing of a few civilians in Podujevo. This was committed by reservists from the ministry. The case was elucidated, criminal charges were filed, and as I've already mentioned, court proceedings are under way in Serbia right now. I also know of the case of the Bljakcori family. I think that this is the month of May. The perpetrators are members of the active police force. The case has been resolved. The perpetrators were arrested. They are in detention. At this moment I don't know what the outcome is, whether the proceedings are already underway. I'm sure they are. Then there is the case in Orahovac where the victims were also three civilians and the perpetrators were the following: One member of the active police force and one member of the reserve police force. I also know of the case in Zegra [phoen], near Gnjilane, where the victims were against civilians and the perpetrators of the crime were members of the army. That was resolved as well. The perpetrators were arrested and handed over to the military judiciary. I'm also aware of the case from Kosovska Mitrovica. Again the victims were civilians. The perpetrators were members of the reserve force of the JSO.
